analysis.one_liner: Restricts banks from owning physical commodities and nonfinancial companies and raises capital requirements for those activities.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2020 with no cosponsors, never received a committee hearing or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have taken away two broad permissions that big bank holding companies currently have. First, it would repeal the 'merchant banking' authority that lets banks own nonfinancial companies the way private equity firms do. Second, it would strip the legal basis banks used to own and store physical commodities like aluminum and oil, and would require the Federal Reserve and the FDIC to jointly approve, by formal rule, any new expansions of bank powers. It would also turn the Fed's 2016 draft rule into binding law, forcing banks to hold more capital against physical commodity trading and merchant banking investments.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday bank depositors and taxpayers, who backstop FDIC-insured banks, benefit from less risk of a big bank's speculative commodity or private-equity losses triggering a bailout. Consumers of commodities like aluminum also stand to gain, since banks that own warehouses can influence the physical supply and raise costs for manufacturers who buy the metal. Smaller firms that compete against banks in trading and investing would face less bank competition.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the merchant banking authority, which lets bank holding companies make private-equity-style investments in nonfinancial companies, removing banks from that business entirely [S2][S3].
Strips the authority bank holding companies have used to own and store physical commodities, ending bank control of things like metal warehouses and energy storage [S2][S3].

Gives the force of law to the Federal Reserve's September 2016 proposed rule, which would impose risk-based capital requirements on financial holding companies' physical commodity activities and merchant banking investments [S2][S3].

Requires the Fed to make any future determination that a new activity is safe for banks jointly with the FDIC, by formal rulemaking rather than unilateral order, adding a second regulator to the decision [S3].
Provides a transition period allowing banks to divest affected shares and assets before complying, reducing market disruption [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large bank holding companies pay: they would have to divest physical commodity businesses and merchant banking stakes, and hold more capital against what remains. That means forgone profits and divestment costs. Bank customers could see some of those forgone returns reflected in bank earnings and could face slightly different credit and trading services.

drawbacks.text: Banks and the Fed have argued that owning commodity businesses can diversify risk and that merchant banking lets banks invest in companies they finance; repealing both removes those tools and could push some activities to less-regulated foreign institutions or shadow markets (general knowledge about the policy debate, informed by the bill's repeal of these authorities) [S3].

The bill's own transition-and-divestment provision acknowledges the change is disruptive: banks would have to sell off substantial assets over time, which could impose costs and shrink services some corporate clients rely on [S3].

The Fed already proposed higher capital requirements for these activities in 2016; critics would say codifying a four-year-old draft rule plus a full repeal goes further than the core safety problem requires [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades real, concentrated bank profits for reduced systemic risk and less bank control over physical commodity supply — a trade-off that favors the public if you believe a bank's speculative commodity or private-equity losses can spread to its insured-deposit business, as the 2008 crisis suggested. The main honest objection is that higher capital requirements alone might have addressed the risk without a full repeal, and that pushing these activities to less-regulated players could simply move the risk elsewhere. The bill never advanced far enough for that debate to happen publicly.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Sean Casten introduced the bill on May 28, 2020, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S1][S5].
The bill had no cosponsors at any point [S4].
No further legislative action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large bank holding companies are better off: they kept their physical commodity businesses and merchant banking authority and avoided the higher capital requirements the bill would have imposed. No one had to argue against the bill on the merits; it simply never moved.

for.name: Rep. Sean Casten
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and no cosponsors signed on from either party, so the partisan shape of support was never tested.

industries.industry: Large bank holding companies with commodity and merchant banking operations
industries.note: The bill would have forced divestment of physical commodity storage and trading businesses and private-equity-style merchant banking stakes, and imposed higher capital requirements on what remained. Banks' profits from these activities come at the price of risk borne by insured depositors and, in a failure, taxpayers, and physical commodity ownership lets banks influence the supply of goods like aluminum that manufacturers buy.

Bank-owned warehouse, pipeline, and energy storage operations would have to be sold or wound down under the bill's divestment transition. These operators can profit by controlling physical supply of commodities that ordinary businesses and consumers ultimately pay for.

industries.industry: Commodity trading houses and nonbank investment firms
industries.note: These firms gain from reduced competition once banks exit physical trading and merchant banking, but some also benefit from buying the assets banks must divest. Their interest runs with the public's only insofar as bank exit reduces market power concentration.
